find:
GRANT UPDATE (state, attempt_count, next_attempt_at, reserved_at, last_attempt_at, completed_at,
  safe_reason_code, updated_at) ON control_owner_push_attempt_heads TO control_room_private_web;
replace: -- MUTATED: the dispatcher's update grant is removed
why: the dispatcher settles every outcome through that column-scoped UPDATE, so without it no item can ever be recorded as delivered and every send fails 42501

a failed send must be re-sendable; without the upgrade clause the retried send is never recorded as delivered, because store.delivered() only updates rows whose state is 'reserved' (postgres-store.ts:58-60). A send-COUNT test cannot see this: deliverOwnerPushV1 sends for BOTH 'reserved' and 'previous_attempt_failed' (delivery.ts:44-46), so the retry's send happens either way. CAUGHT: tests/owner-push-dispatch-postgres.test.ts, 'a send that failed then succeeded leaves the ledger delivered, and dedupes the next pass'. It drives the real dispatcher through a 503 and then a 201 on real PostgreSQL as the production private-web login, then reads owner_web_push_deliveries on an INDEPENDENT connection and asserts state=delivered -- plus the consequence, that a later dispatch of the same item is deduped rather than pushed again. MEASURED with the mutation applied: the ledger reads 'failed' and the test fails on that assertion; clean, it passes.

find: WHERE tenant_id=$1 AND action_inbox_id=ANY($3::text[]) AND state='pending'
why: the reserve is the compare-and-set that makes a claim exclusive; without the state test two racing dispatchers both reserve the same item and both send -- NOT independently detectable, and recorded as defence in depth. The reserve runs inside the same transaction as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so the lock already serialises two racing dispatchers and this state test is a second condition on top of it, not the only one. The two-dispatcher race test proves exclusivity and does fail if the WHOLE claim/reserve pairing is broken (verified by mutating the SELECT's state filter instead), but not by mutating this one. -- MEASURED: not independently detectable. With the reserve's own state='pending' compare-and-set in the same transaction, the FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lock is redundant with it; removing either one alone leaves every test green. Both are kept deliberately because they fail differently (a blocking claim under a long send vs a duplicate send under any scheduler change), and the original defect was the two being in SEPARATE transactions, not either being absent.

find: WHERE h.tenant_id=$1 AND h.state='pending' AND h.next_attempt_at<=$2
replace: WHERE h.tenant_id=$1 AND h.state IN ('pending','reserved') AND h.next_attempt_at<=$2
why: only 'pending' is claimable, so a 'reserved' row must not consume a slot of the claim's LIMIT. The reserve statement repeats state=pending in its WHERE clause, so such a row cannot be reserved twice -- that later guard prevents a DUPLICATE but not a WASTED SLOT, and the claim transaction commits before the send, so the row holds no lock and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED does not skip it either. CAUGHT: tests/owner-push-dispatch-postgres.test.ts, 'a reserved head younger than the stale window does not consume the claim's limit'. A reserved head sorting first in the window, with dispatch(1): shipped selects the due pending head and sends it; widened selects the reserved head, the UPDATE's pending predicate filters it out, and the batch is empty. The full 64-row window is the same shape at the production CLAIM_LIMIT. Both on real PostgreSQL as the production private-web login. MEASURED with the mutation applied: dispatch(1) returns [] and the test fails; clean, it returns one outcome for the pending head.

find:
WHERE h.tenant_id=$1 AND h.state='reserved' AND h.reserved_at<=$2
        AND i.tenant_id=h.tenant_id AND i.id=h.action_inbox_id AND i.state='open'
replace:
WHERE h.tenant_id=$1 AND h.state='reserved' AND h.reserved_at<=$2 AND false
        AND i.tenant_id=h.tenant_id AND i.id=h.action_inbox_id AND i.state='open'
why: a dispatcher killed between the reservation and the settle leaves a row no tick can ever pick up, so that stall is never pushed for at all

find: const terminal = disposition === "delivered" || disposition === "failed" || spent >= OWNER_PUSH_ATTEMPT_LIMIT_V1;
why: the attempt bound must stop retrying for good, so a permanently dead endpoint cannot send for ever

find:
if (!sendFailure) {
      // No subscription left by the time this item was sent to.
replace:
if (false) {
      // No subscription left by the time this item was sent to.
why: no-subscription is distinguished from send-failure by the failure report, never by the counters alone. This is the RESIDUAL path only -- the pre-claim gate handles the common case before anything is claimed, so this branch is reached only when a subscription vanished mid-batch, which the new 'subscription that vanishes mid-batch' test drives explicitly. The earlier version of this entry was recorded as NOT independently detectable because no test installed zero subscriptions at all; that is now the 50-item no-subscription stress test, so this branch is reachable and this entry bites.
a delivered head must be terminal: without this a caller can rewind it to pending and re-alert the owner for a stall they already answered
the attempt count may never be rewound, so a delivered item cannot be made to look like it was never tried

find: attempt_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (attempt_count BETWEEN 0 AND 8),
replace: attempt_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (attempt_count >= 0),
why: the bound is also enforced by the column, independently of the guard, so a path the guard misses still cannot retry for ever

a stored deep link may only be one of the three product paths, so a phone can never open an off-site URL. 0226 grants the private-web role INSERT on this table and 0225's guard is BEFORE UPDATE only, so a direct INSERT is inside the boundary the production role really has -- which is exactly why no test that reached the table through the dispatcher ever exercised this. CAUGHT: tests/owner-push-dispatch-postgres.test.ts, 'the owner web login cannot write a head with an off-path link, or two heads for one item'. It INSERTs //evil.invalid as the production private-web login and asserts SQLSTATE 23514, plus three more shapes MEASURED to be distinguishing: /needs-me/../admin, /Needs-me and /admin/settings (each is admitted by the widened CHECK). A scheme-qualified URL was measured and deliberately excluded -- it does not start with a slash, so both spellings refuse it and it proves nothing. MEASURED with the mutation applied: Missing expected rejection.

(tenant_id, action_inbox_id) is what makes one Needs-you item own exactly one push head for the life of the installation, and 0225's guard then forbids changing it on UPDATE. Widening the key to admit a third column lets one item own several heads, so a single stall can be pushed more than once. CAUGHT: the same test as #11. It INSERTs /needs-me then /morning for one tenant/item as the production private-web login and asserts SQLSTATE 23505 on the second, then that exactly one row survives holding the link that was actually written. MEASURED with the mutation applied: Missing expected rejection: a second head for one item; clean, both refusals hold.
a push failure is reported as a bare reason code; a raw message would carry the push endpoint URL and the quoted task text into the host log
a down push service at host startup must not fail the host's startup path; the items are still in the inbox and the next tick picks them up
a 404/410 means the browser subscription is gone and has already been removed, so the item must stop for good rather than spend the bounded attempts reaching nothing

THE FIX for the review's blocking bug. Without the pre-claim gate, a tenant with no subscribed browser claims each item, spends an attempt, and 0225's guard then refuses the release's decrement -- so the increments stick, the whole budget burns in about four minutes at the production 30s interval, and the item sits at 'pending' with attempt_count=8, permanently unclaimable and never delivered even after the owner subscribes. The gate means an item with nobody to send it to is never claimed, so it spends no attempt and heals the moment a subscription exists.

the re-check must be in the FUTURE. Leaving next_attempt_at at now re-claims the item on the very next tick, which is what burned the budget four times faster than the backoff schedule says; the assertion that every waiting item's next_attempt_at is later than the clock is the one that bites

find:
WHERE tenant_id=$1 AND state='pending' AND next_attempt_at<=$2
      RETURNING action_inbox_id,attempt_count
replace:
WHERE tenant_id=$1 AND next_attempt_at<=$2
      RETURNING action_inbox_id,attempt_count
why: the deferral must touch only 'pending' rows. A reserved row belongs to a dispatcher that is mid-send RIGHT NOW, and moving its next_attempt_at under it is how a live send gets rescheduled by a second dispatcher that decided there was nobody to send to

the reason code is what an operator reads, and 'waiting for a subscription' and 'the push endpoint is unavailable' call for opposite actions: one is fixed by Settings, the other by waiting. The assertion on owner_push_no_subscription is the one that bites

the status must be checked BEFORE store.delivered(), which is a terminal, non-retryable write to the 0174 ledger. Recording it for a response outside 2xx would settle the item as delivered and the phone would never ring for that stall. Unreachable through the real web-push library, which REJECTS on non-2xx -- which is exactly why the invariant has to be enforced by this code rather than by an external library's undocumented contract

the allow list must be matched on the WHOLE host, not a suffix or a substring. A suffix test admits ANY host under a vendor's domain, which is not a push service and is an SSRF; the refused-endpoint table has evil.invalid, a suffixed apple host, a prefixed fcm host and a Windows wildcard abuse for exactly this
HTTPS only. An http endpoint would carry the VAPID-signed request in clear text and would reach a different service entirely; the refused table has an http://fcm.googleapis.com entry for this

the allow list must be enforced at SUBSCRIBE time, the earliest and cheapest point, so a refused endpoint never reaches the database. channel.ts would still refuse it at send time, so this entry is defence in depth rather than the only guard -- but the database-side check in 0227 is a third independent one, and this is the one that keeps the row out of existence

this is the check that actually stops the outbound request, so it is the one that is not optional. A row written before the allow list existed, or by anything else holding INSERT, would otherwise be dialled by the dispatcher on its own schedule with the VAPID private key resident on the web process

the database is the third independent copy of the allow list. policy.ts refuses at subscribe, channel.ts refuses at send, and this refuses the row itself -- which is what holds against a writer that is neither the application nor a future bug in it

a fragment is never part of a real push endpoint and a browser never sends one, so a fragment means the string is not a push URL. NOTE: this is deliberately only the FRAGMENT, not the query. An earlier version of this entry refused '?' as well, which would have refused every real Windows Notification Services subscription -- a real WNS channel URL carries its token in the query (`https://<label>.notify.windows.com/?token=...`, per Microsoft's own documentation). A query is not an SSRF vector here because the host is read from the authority, which ends at the first '/', '?' or '#', so `https://evil.invalid/?next=web.push.apple.com` is refused on the host and not on the query.
a credential in the URL is credential material, not a shape question, and the userinfo section is exactly where an allow-listed host would hide behind an attacker-chosen prefix
